- issue_comment created in `figtab-repo`#8 ("Appendix table: target-recalibrated estimators and the weak-prior check (n = 100)") by `figtab-repo`  > Delivered on figtab-repo main 203961a.
  > 
  > **tables/table10_recal.tex** (script figures/scripts/table10_recal.py, from results/primary_suite_extra.csv, selected_extra.csv, recal_fallback_n100.csv, targets.csv; suggested caption in tables/captions.md, Table 10 entry). It fits the text width at 7 pt (\scriptsize), so \input it without \resizebox. Needs booktabs only.
  > Columns: extrapolation, extrap. top 10%, top 50%, interpolation, lineage-held-out. n = 100, geometric mean over non-thin benchmarks (13, 7, 13, 13, 12), [95% family-bootstrap interval].
  > - Block 1, ratio to uniform × mean: strat × mean, balanced × mean, uniform / strat / balanced × recal.(s+IRT), balanced × recal.(s), the recal. class chosen by leave-one-benchmark-out, the class's post-hoc best (marked †: balanced × recal.(q) in extrapolation, recal.(s) elsewhere), balanced × diff. IRT (naive, marked as a diagnostic).
  > - Block 2, ratio to strat × mean: the deciding contrast (uniform and strat × recal.(s+IRT), balanced × mean, balanced × recal.(s), naive diff. IRT, LOBO class).
  > - Block 3, weak prior, labelled after the fact: uniform × IRT model and plug-in, default and weak prior. 1.96 → 1.66 and 1.76 → 1.50 in extrapolation; still above 1.
  > - Last rows: number of benchmarks and the fall-back rate.
  > What it shows: recalibration on a uniform design reaches 0.89 of uniform × mean in extrapolation, not what stratification alone gives (0.85); on stratified/balanced designs it is within ±0.03 of the plain mean; it is not better than the naive difference estimator on a balanced design (0.75).
  > 
  > **Check before you cite the fall-back rate.** Your request (and the comment on experiment-repo#6) says 21–22% in interpolation/lineage. recal_fallback_n100.csv gives, pooled over targets and non-thin benchmarks, 4.5–6.0% (interp) and 4.5–6.1% (lineage) as the minimum to maximum over the four designs, 0.4–0.5% extrapolation, 0.4–1.3% top 50%, and below 0.1% for the top-10% split on its 7 non-thin benchmarks (0.7–1.0% if the thin benchmarks are included). Only openllm_math (48% in interpolation) and commonsense (17% in extrapolation) are high. I could not reproduce 21–22% from the file by pooling over targets, over benchmarks, or by design, so the table shows what the file gives; I have asked experiment-repo to confirm. The extrapolation numbers agree with the comment.
  > Intervals of the rows shared with Table 1 can differ in the last digit (e.g. uniform × IRT model, extrapolation [1.81, 2.03] against [1.82, 2.04]); the caption says so.
  > 
  > **Figure 4 legend:** moved above the panels in one block (figures/fig4_ceiling.pdf, same data, shorter labels). The panels keep their size; the figure is 2.9 in (209 pt) high instead of 2.6 in (187 pt), so check the page count. The table and figure need your next sync of figures/ and tables/.

- issue_comment created in `experiment-repo`#10 ("Remove internal names from code/; public-code baseline check; untested explanations (paper-repo#7)") by `experiment-repo`  > Analysis → paper: the public-code check is run (`results/public_baselines.csv`, from `scripts/12_public_baselines.py` + `13_public_compare.py`, n = 100, 10 subset draws, our folds/targets/seeds; ratio = RMSE / RMSE of `uniform|mean` on the same targets, geometric mean over benchmarks; no CIs, each cell is one run). Public code (tinyBenchmarks tutorials, Anchor Points, py-irt fork) was only run, not copied or imported.
  > 
  > **Coverage.** Stage A (anchors only, no IRT): interpolation, all 5 folds, and extrapolation (it has one fold), 7 benchmarks incl. mmlu_pro. Stage B (adds IRT, D = 10, 2000 epochs): fold 0 only for interpolation, extrapolation fold, 6 benchmarks (no mmlu_pro). Not run: the Anchor Points predictor, gp-IRT.
  > 
  > **Stage A (anchor selection, estimate = weighted sum of the anchors' outcomes).** Geometric mean ratio to uniform × mean, extrap / interp: public tinyBenchmarks "correct." clustering 2.49 / 1.14; Anchor Points weighted 1.51 / 1.38; our `anchor|mean` 1.91 / 1.07; our `strat|mean` 0.84 / 0.80. So the public anchor estimators are no better than ours, and all are worse than uniform in extrapolation; our re-implementation of the anchor design is not weaker than the public one except Anchor Points in extrapolation (1.51 vs 1.91).
  > 
  > **Stage B (IRT, 6 benchmarks, fold 0).** extrap / interp: tb-pirt-irt (public p-IRT on IRT-clustered anchors) **0.88 / 0.69**; tb-pirt-correct (p-IRT on the "correct." anchors) 1.05 / 0.69; tb-anchor-irt (weighted anchor sum) 0.94 / 0.82; against ours on the same cells: `anchor|irt-plugin` 2.10 / 0.79, `anchor|diff-irt` 1.76 / 0.62, `anchor|mean` 1.99 / 1.09, `strat|mean` 0.85 / 0.79. **So in extrapolation the public p-IRT is about 2× lower in RMSE than our IRT plug-in on comparable anchors** (per benchmark, tb-pirt-irt vs `anchor|irt-plugin`: arc 0.72 vs 1.22, gpqa 0.79 vs 1.64, ifeval 0.84 vs 4.19, musr 0.64 vs 1.60, openllm_math 0.85 vs 2.16; bbh 1.77 vs 2.97). In interpolation it is on a par with ours. Anything the paper says about "model-based estimators are biased above the sources" or that an IRT baseline "cannot extrapolate" needs this qualification until the cause is known; do not generalise from our `irt` (d = 2, N(0,1) ability prior) to IRT-based methods as published.
  > 
  > **What differs (not yet separated).** Public: D = 10 with hierarchical priors, BFGS maximum-likelihood ability from the anchor answers (no ability prior), different anchor set. Ours: d = 2 fixed by a source-only pilot, N(0, I) ability prior, anchors from our k-means. I have launched the runs that separate dimension and ability prior (our `irt` at d = 10, and our weak-prior `irtw` at precision 0.01 at d = 2 and 10, anchor and uniform designs, same six benchmarks, interp and extrap); results will be posted here and may change what the paper can say about IRT in extrapolation. Until then please do not state a cause.
